narrative:
The model determined that you have a 78% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence; being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. Your LSAT score of 26 was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failing, especially when compared to the average of 37 among students who were accepted. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.10 was the third most influential element. While this score did slightly improve the model’s outlook, it was not nearly enough to offset the other two signals.

Taken together, your low year-three ranking and modest LSAT score told the model you would most likely struggle to pass the bar, outweighing the modest positive nudge from your GPA.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT and aiming for a substantially higher score, combined with demonstrable improvement in your academic performance, would be the clearest way to shift future predictions in your favor. Consider targeted test-prep resources or academic support programs before reapplying.
